system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2187-02-26 23:26:00 to 2187-03-02 15:49:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease, short bowel syndrome, and SVC syndrome was admitted with worsening facial and neck swelling, headaches, nausea, and blurred vision due to recurrent superior vena cava obstruction. An open SVC reconstruction with bovine pericardial patch and endarterectomy was performed successfully. Postoperatively, she developed a hematoma at the left groin line site requiring removal, and experienced a drop in hemoglobin requiring transfusion and subsequent Epogen administration. Her pain and anxiety were managed with morphine elixir, benzodiazepines, and antihistamines. She improved steadily, was ambulating independently, and was discharged home in good condition with sternal precautions, anticoagulation, and follow-up planned with her PCP in four days.
problems: Chronic venous embolism and thrombosis of other thoracic veins
Chronic venous embolism and thrombosis of subclavian veins
Chronic venous embolism and thrombosis of internal jugular veins
Nonspecific abnormal findings in stool contents
Personal history of allergy to other specified medicinal agents

17. Lidoderm 5 %(700 mg/patch) Adhesive Patch, Medicated Sig: 
One (1)  Topical Q 12 HRS.  
18. fondaparinux 7.5 mg/0.6 mL Syringe Sig: One (1)  
Subcutaneous once a day for 1 months.

If there is continues clinical concern for bowel obstruction, consider CT, if

PLACEMENT OF A PERIPHERAL VENOUS LINE.

The patient was consented for monitored conscious sedation after risks and

prior to the procedure according to the ___ policy.  The patient
was placed on a fluoroscopic table in supine position.  Skin of the left upper

left upper extremity with extensive collateralization.  A vein was
successfully accessed using 21-gauge needle followed by insertion of a 2.5
___ stiffener for a 4 ___ sheath which was advanced into the accessed

were unsuitable for advancement of PICC line.  2.5 ___ sheath was secured

CONCLUSION:  Placement of a 2.5 ___ sheath into the left upper extremity

Extensive and multifocal ___ venoocclusive disease of the deep and

INDICATION:  ___ woman status post SVC thrombectomy with vein patch,
now with low-grade temperature.  Request is to evaluate for source of sepsis

COMPARISON:  Reference is made to the postoperative CT abdomen and pelvis
dated ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Multidetector CT-acquired axial images were obtained from the
skull base to the level of the distal femoral diaphysis following
administration of intravenous contrast.  Note, the patient has a contrast
allergy and was premedicated for the procedure.  Intravenous contrast was
injected via the left arm at a rate of 2 cc/sec via a hand injection.There
were no early complications.

CT OF THORAX:
  
There is ground-glass opacity with bronchiectasis and bronchial wall
thickening noted involving the posterior segment of the right upper lobe.  A
similar, although less advanced appearance was noted on a previous CT thorax
from ___.  Further areas of scarring and mild bronchiectasis are seen
involving the posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe.  There has been
resolution of the previously noted right-sided pleural effusion and marked
decrease in size of the left-sided pleural effusion since the prior study of
___.  There has also been significant reexpansion of the previously
noted bibasal atelectasis.  

The patient is status post median sternotomy with excision extension above the
sternal notch.  There is a serpiginous fluid collection extending from the
level of the right lobe of thyroid which extends inferiorly to the level of
the sternal notch where a small fluid collection tracks anteriorly to lie
anterior to the manubrium sternum.  The deep part of the fluid collection
extends deep to the medial end of the clavicle and becomes confluent with a
larger fluid collection deep to the sternum which appears to communicate with
the previously noted pericardial effusion.  
The pericardial effusion has increased in size since the prior study.  The
___ attenuation value of the fluid again is consistent with complex
fluid.  There is apparent enhancement of the anteromedial portion of the
pericardium which may represent the reconstructed component. A more
circumscribed fluid collection deep to the xiphoid process noted on the prior
study has decreased in size from 19 x 29 mm to 16 x 12 mm (4:124). 
A 14 mm radiopaque density is noted in the soft tissues of the left anterior
chest (4:46).  Findings are suggestive of a retained catheter fragment.  This
fragment was present on a previous PA radiograph from ___. 

THORACIC VASCULAR STRUCTURES:
The aortic arch and great vessels outline normally.  Normal appearance of both
common carotid arteries.  The right internal jugular vein is markedly narrowed
by the right cervical fluid collection but appears contiguous with the
attenuated right subclavian vein.  The short right brachiocephalic vein then
descends and joins the reconstructed SVC, which  appears patent. The medial
aspect of the reconstructed SVC is indented by an oval fluid collection
measuring 21 x 53 mm, the anterior end of which communicates with the
pericardial fluid collection.  

On the left side, the left internal jugular vein is markedly attenuated and
appears to drain into a left mediastinal collateral vein.  No patent left
brachiocephalic vein is identified.  
Numerous 1 cm lymph nodes are identified in the pretracheal and subcarinal
positions, likely reactive. Note is made of an enlarged 15 mm right hilar
lymph node, likely reactive to the adjacent inflammatory change within the
right upper lobe (4:94).

There are extensive left chest wall and left flank collaterals opacified by
the left arm contrast injection.  
 

CT OF ABDOMEN:  No focal liver lesions. There has been a previous
cholecystectomy.  Normal appearance of the pancreas and spleen. There is no
ascites.  Enteral anastamotic clips are seen in the region of the right
subhepatic space in keeping with previous right colonic resection and primary
anastomosis.  The IVC and aorta are patent and normal in appearance.  Normal
appearance of the right atrium.

CT OF PELVIS:    There is expansion of the inferior portion of the left rectus
sheath which contains a high density air and fluid collection.  The collection
measures 57 ___ units, and findings are in keeping with organized blood
or possible contrast from previous extravasation from the left common femoral
line injection.  The collection measures 7 x 3 mm in the axial plane.  More
inferiorly, there is a multiloculated fluid collection measuring 3.2 x 5.9 cm
which indents the bladder and displaces it to the right side.  There is
significant stranding of the surrounding fat.  Findings are in keeping with
organizing collections from the previous contrast extravasation from the left
groin access line from the CT of ___.  
There is soft tissue stranding along the site of the previous right common
femoral vein catheter.  

ABDOMINAL/PELVIC VASCULAR STRUCTURES:
Normal appearance of both common iliac, external and internal iliac arteries. 
Normal appearance of both common femoral arteries.There is further extensive
venous occlusion involving the external iliac veins bilaterally .Both internal
iliac veins are patent.  There is extensive pelvic venous collateralization
with a large cross midline collateral noted extending from the right internal
iliac vein to the left internal iliac vein.
Normal appearance of the superficial femoral artery and vein in the upper
thigh.


OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:  Median sternotomy as described:  No lytic or sclerotic
destructive bone lesions are identified.

IMPRESSION:
1. Increase in size of the pericardial effusion.  
2. Fluid collections on the right side of neck and anterior mediastinum as
described.  
3. Attenuated right subclavian and right brachiocephalic vein but patent  into
the SVC.  
4. The right internal jugular vein is compressed by the fluid collection
although appears patent. 
5.  The left internal jugular vein is patent but narrows markedly in its
inferior portion and does not communicate with an occluded left
brachiocephalic vein and rather drains via a mediastinal collateral.  
6. The left subclavian vein is occluded. 
7.  There is occlusion of both external iliac veins with extensive internal
iliac vein collaterals within the pelvis. 
8. The right CFV drains via a large collateral into the internal iliac vein
which is patent to the IVC and this route has potential for central venous
access if needed.
9.  Inflammatory change in the posterior segment of right upper lobe has
increased since the prior study.
10. Pelvic fluid collections and rectus sheath expansion as described.

The staff radiologist has reviewed the images and the report.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your surgical team doctors. I understand you came in with a fever and chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up at 3 a.m. with a high fever—up to 103. It’s down a bit now, but I still feel awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also mentioned right-sided chest pain and chills. Any shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Only when I move or take a deep breath. It’s been there since I left the hospital last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll check your lungs and run some tests. Given your recent surgery, we need to rule out infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had fevers before after surgeries. But this one feels different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re taking it seriously. We’ve ordered blood work and a chest X-ray. We’ll also do an ultrasound on your right arm because of the swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My fingers were numb earlier, but that’s better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That could be related to circulation. We’ll monitor that. Let’s get your vitals checked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. White blood cell count is a bit low at 3.9, and your hemoglobin is 7.4, which is down from before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? Should I get a transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching it closely. No transfusion needed right now. Your electrolytes are off too—low calcium and magnesium. We’ll give supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I always run low on those. My Crohn’s makes it hard to absorb nutrients.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep adjusting your IV fluids and supplements. Now, the ultrasound showed a clot in your right basilic vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another clot? But I’m on blood thinners!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but because of your HIT history, we’re using fondaparinux instead of heparin. This clot is in a superficial vein, so we’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it go away on its own?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely, with the blood thinner. We’re more concerned about your chest. The X-ray shows some lingering changes in your right lung.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re starting you on IV antibiotics—vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam—just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to a lot of antibiotics. Are these safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we checked your allergies. These are safe for you. We’ll watch for any reaction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your leg ultrasound showed no DVTs. Both legs are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about clots spreading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too. But your arms are more concerning. We’re planning a CT scan to check your graft and lung.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to contrast. Won’t that be a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll pre-medicate you to reduce the risk. It’s important we see what’s going on in your chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT is done. There’s a small increase in fluid around your heart, but the graft looks patent and not infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the fluid dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not immediately. It’s likely reactive. But we’re watching it. The lung shows more inflammation in the right upper lobe—consistent with infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it is pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. We’ll continue IV antibiotics and switch to oral later. We also found a small retained catheter fragment in your left chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should that come out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. It’s not causing issues. We’ll note it for future procedures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fever has come down. You’ve been afebrile for 12 hours now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Does that mean I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a good sign. We’ll keep the antibiotics going and monitor your labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried to place a PICC line for easier access, but your veins are too damaged. We had to use a temporary sheath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve always been hard to stick. It’s frustrating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. The radiologist noted extensive blockages and collaterals. We’ll manage with what we have.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT confirmed the lung infection is improving with treatment. The graft remains open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart fluid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but stable. No signs of infection in the graft. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been fever-free for over 48 hours. We’re ready to send you home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful! What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the oral antibiotic—levofloxacin—for two weeks. Take pain meds as needed. Watch for fever, redness at incisions, or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood thinner?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue fondaparinux daily for a month. We’ll follow up with your PCP in four days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad this is behind me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Call us if anything changes. Rest and take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease, short bowel syndrome, and recent SVC repair presented with fever, chills, and right-sided chest pain. She was found to have a superficial thrombus in the right basilic vein and evidence of right upper lobe pneumonia on imaging. She was treated with IV antibiotics, which were later transitioned to oral levofloxacin, and continued on fondaparinux for HIT. Her fever resolved within 48 hours, and she improved clinically. A PICC line could not be placed due to extensive venous occlusive disease. She was discharged home in stable condition with a plan for outpatient antibiotic completion and follow-up.
